do-i-need-to-hire-another-employee.html.text:
← Shift roster builder

Do I need to hire another employee? Test the schedule first

"We are short-staffed" can mean three different things: not enough hours in the team, not enough people at the times you need them, or one person everything depends on. Only the first is fixed by adding a person at random. Checking takes a few minutes, before you spend money on a job post.

Open the free roster builder

Step 1: hours needed against hours available

Multiply each shift's length by the people it needs and add up the week. Then add every person's weekly hour limit. If the first number is larger, no schedule can cover the week, whatever the arrangement. The builder prints this warning for you when it happens.

A worked example: a four-person salon

The numbers below are invented and were produced by the builder itself; the page's tests re-run them, so they cannot drift from the tool.

PersonWageWeekly limitAvailable
Maya$2440 hTue–Sat 9–19
Jo$2036 hMon–Fri 9–19
Priya$1824 hThu–Sun 10–20
Sam$1520 hMon–Sat 9–19

The shop needs two people 9–2 and two people 2–7 on weekdays, three people 10–6 on Saturday and one person 10–4 on Sunday: 130 hours a week. The team's limits add up to 120 hours, so the answer to step 1 is already "no, not as it stands".

Step 2: see where it breaks

The builder fills 97 of the 130 hours and leaves 6 shifts open (33 hours): two Monday afternoon places, Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday afternoons, and one Saturday place. For each one it says why. Monday afternoon, for example: two people are free, but one would break the 10-hour rest rule and one is at their weekly limit. Sunday is only coverable by Priya, so if she is sick the shop is closed.

Step 3: test the hire before you make it

Adding a person to the list costs nothing. With one extra part-timer at $17 an hour, up to 30 hours, free any time, the week goes from 6 open shifts to 1 open shift (5 hours). The new person works 28 hours and total payroll rises from $1,904 to $2,380. The builder's own "what if we hired" test, which assumes an average wage of $19.25 and 40 hours, gives the same picture: 28 hours covered, 5 still open, about $545 more payroll a week. That is the price of those 28 hours, and the figure to compare with what the uncovered chairs would earn.

Two things to read off that result. The remaining gap is a Monday afternoon place: Maya and Priya do not work Mondays, so only Jo, Sam and the new person can. That suggests asking for Monday availability in the job post, not just hours. And it shows who the week depends on: with Maya out, 28 more hours go uncovered, more than anyone else.

Try it with your own team

Questions

How do I know if I need to hire another employee?

Add up the hours your shifts require and compare them with the combined weekly hour limits of your current team. If the shifts need more than the team can give, hiring or cutting shifts is unavoidable. If the team has enough hours on paper but shifts still go uncovered, the problem is availability, not headcount, and a person with wider availability fixes it better than more hours do.

Is it cheaper to pay overtime or hire a part-timer?

Overtime hours cost a premium, often time and a half, on top of the wage. A part-timer costs the wage but also carries hiring, training and payroll-tax costs. For a few short weeks overtime is usually cheaper; for a gap that repeats every week, a hire is. Test both by running the schedule with and without the extra person.

Does the tool say whether my schedule is legal?

No. It applies the rest, hour and overtime rules you type in. It does not know your local scheduling-notice, break or minor-labor laws.

No warranty. Free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. This page is general information, not legal, tax or financial advice, and it does not tell you what scheduling law requires of you. Rules vary by place and change; check current guidance or ask a qualified professional. The example is invented.

Everything the roster builder does runs in your browser; your staff list is never uploaded. Free and open source: support is entirely optional. Related: how to make an employee schedule, the shift-cover optimizer.

how-to-avoid-clopening.html.text:
← Shift roster builder

How to avoid clopening: what a rest gap between shifts costs

A clopening is a late close followed by an early open: someone locks up at 11pm and unlocks at 6am. The standard fix is a minimum rest gap between any two of a person's shifts. Owners worry that a rule like that leaves shifts empty or raises payroll. We measured it.

Open the free roster builder

The experiment

The roster builder's built-in invented example: a seven-person cafe, 32 shifts, 235 hours to cover, a 40-hour overtime line, and each person's own availability. Only the rest gap changed between runs; everything else is the tool's defaults.

Minimum rest gapShifts left openHours coveredPayroll
None (0 h)3211 of 235$3,525
8 h3216$3,620
10 h3216$3,622
12 h3216$3,630
14 h6212$3,578

What it shows

For this cafe, a rest gap anywhere from 8 to 12 hours cost about $100 a week more than no rule and did not leave a single extra shift open. The search simply gave the awkward close-then-open pairs to different people. At 14 hours the rule starts to bite: the same staff can no longer cover three more shifts. So the question to ask of your own week is where your cliff is, not whether a rule is affordable in general. This is one invented example, not a benchmark, and your availability decides your numbers.

Find the cliff in your own week

How to do it by hand

1. Mark every close and every open

List who works each closing shift, then check the next morning's opens for the same names.

2. Swap one side of each pair

Move either the close or the open to someone who is free and not already near their weekly limit. Do the people with the narrowest availability first.

3. Watch the week boundary

Sunday night's close and Monday morning's open are the pair most often missed. The roster builder can read last week's roster CSV so the rule holds across Monday.

Questions

What does clopening mean in scheduling?

It means working a closing shift and then the opening shift the next morning, leaving little time to sleep. A minimum rest gap between shifts is the usual way to prevent it.

How many hours of rest should be between shifts?

There is no single answer. Some employers use 8 to 12 hours as policy and some places regulate it for certain workers. Check the rules where you operate. The roster builder lets you set the gap and will not break it.

No warranty. Free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. This page is general information, not legal, tax or financial advice, and it does not tell you what scheduling law requires of you. The example is invented and the numbers come from running this tool's own engine on it.

how-to-make-an-employee-schedule.html.text:
← Shift roster builder

How to make an employee schedule that covers every shift

Most small-business schedules are made on Sunday night from memory, a spreadsheet and a few text messages. The same four things go wrong: a shift nobody noticed was uncovered, someone scheduled on a day they cannot work, an avoidable overtime week, and the same two people getting all the good (or all the bad) shifts. Doing the steps in the right order fixes most of it.

Open the free roster builder

The method

1. Write the shifts down as requirements, not as names

For each day: start, end, how many people it takes. "Mon–Fri 6–2, two people, open" is a requirement; "Ana and Ben on opens" is already a decision. Keeping them apart is what lets you see the real total of hours you must cover.

2. Write down each person's hard limits

Availability windows, the most hours they can or want to work, and the fewest you have promised. Days not on the list count as unavailable. If the weekly limits of everyone together are smaller than the hours to cover, no schedule works and it is better to learn that before the week starts.

3. Apply the hard rules before you think about money

A person must be free for the whole shift, cannot be in two places, needs enough rest since their last shift, and has a cap on days in a row. These are not preferences. The most constrained shifts (the ones only one or two people can work) go first, or the easy shifts will use up exactly the people the hard ones need.

4. Then trade cost, overtime and fairness

Among the schedules that obey the rules, an overtime hour costs a premium, so keep people under the threshold when someone else is free. Giving every hour to the cheapest person is cheap on paper and loses staff, so a fair share of hours and a minimum for the people you have promised them belong in the score too.

5. Look for the single points of failure

Remove each person in turn and see which shifts go uncovered. Anyone whose absence leaves a shift open is who the week depends on: they need a backup, or a wider availability from someone else.

A worked example

An invented café has seven people and 32 shifts to fill across the week, 235 hours in all, with a 10-hour rest rule, a 40-hour overtime line and everyone's own availability. Filling shifts in time order with the first free name on the list leaves 7 shifts open, 58 hours nobody is scheduled for. The roster builder, given the same people and rules, leaves 3 shifts open and tells you why for each: for example the Monday lunch has four people free, but all four are already at their weekly limit. It also reports that taking out any one of Ana, Dev or Gus leaves 40 more hours uncovered, so those three are the café's single points of failure. The fix is a decision for the owner: ask Fay or Cleo for wider availability, add an hour limit exception, or shorten a shift.

Try it with your own week

Questions

What is a clopening and why do schedules avoid it?

A clopening is a closing shift followed by an opening shift the next morning, leaving very little time to sleep. Some places limit it by law or policy with a minimum rest gap between shifts, often somewhere around 8 to 11 hours. Check what applies where you operate; the roster builder lets you set the gap and will not break it.

How do I avoid overtime when making a schedule?

Count each person's hours across the whole pay week, not shift by shift, and give the marginal shift to someone who is still under the threshold even if they cost slightly more per hour. One overtime hour at time and a half costs more than an extra hour for anyone paid up to half as much again as the person already at the limit.

How far in advance do I have to post a schedule?

It depends on where you operate. Some cities and states have predictive-scheduling or fair-workweek rules with advance-notice periods and pay for late changes, usually aimed at larger retail, food-service and hospitality employers. This tool does not check them, so look up the rules for your location.

No warranty. Free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. This page is general information, not legal, tax or financial advice, and it does not tell you what scheduling law requires of you. Rules vary by place and change; check current guidance or ask a qualified professional. The example is invented.

how-to-reduce-overtime-in-a-schedule.htm.text:
← Shift roster builder

How to reduce overtime in a weekly schedule: what the overtime line costs

Overtime is rarely planned. It happens when the same few people are the only ones free for the long shifts, and the schedule is built one shift at a time. The fix is to count hours as you assign and, where you can, hand the shift to someone still under the line. We measured how much overtime one invented week still needs, and what it costs, at three different lines.

Open the free roster builder

The experiment

The roster builder's built-in invented example: a seven-person cafe, 32 shifts, 235 hours to cover, each person's own availability and weekly hour limit, a 10-hour rest gap. Only the overtime line changed between runs (hours past the line are paid at 1.5 times the wage); everything else is the tool's defaults.

Overtime lineOvertime hours in the best rosterHours coveredPayroll
30 h30216 of 235$3,890
35 h13216$3,739
40 h0216$3,622

What it shows

At a 40-hour line this cafe can be covered with no overtime at all. Moving the line to 35 hours, the same schedule can no longer avoid 13 hours of premium pay, and at 30 hours it is 30 hours, about $270 more a week than at 40. Coverage did not change in any run: the search protected covered hours first and let the premium fall where it was cheapest. So the useful question about your own week is how many hours sit just past your line, and who could take them. This is one invented example, not a benchmark, and your availability decides your numbers.

See the overtime in your own week

How to do it by hand

1. Keep a running total per person

Write each person's hours beside their name and update it after every shift you assign.

2. Fill the hardest shifts first

Give the shifts few people can work to those people early, while they have room, then fill the easy shifts around them.

3. Split the last long shift

If the only person free would cross the line, cut the shift into two shorter ones for two people instead. The roster builder does this when it is cheaper.

Questions

How do you reduce overtime when making a schedule?

Count each person's hours as you assign shifts and give the next shift to someone who is free and still under the overtime line. When everyone available is near the line, split the long shift or hire cover. The roster builder prices overtime into its search, so it gives hours to people under the line before it pays a premium.

When does overtime start?

It depends on where you operate and who the worker is. Many places count hours over 40 in a week, and some also count hours over a daily limit. Check the rules that apply to you. The roster builder lets you enter your own weekly and daily lines.

No warranty. Free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. This page is general information, not legal, tax or financial advice, and it does not tell you what overtime law requires of you. The example is invented and the numbers come from running this tool's own engine on it.

index.html.text:
SHIFT ROSTER BUILDER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Build this week's schedule without the spreadsheet puzzle

List the shifts you need covered and your people with their availability, weekly hour limits and wages. The tool assigns people to shifts so that every shift is covered if it can be, nobody works outside their availability, gets less rest than you allow, or goes into overtime when someone cheaper is free. Shifts it cannot fill come back with the reason, and it shows who the week depends on. Download the roster as a CSV.

Your staff list never leaves this browser tab. Planning aid, not legal, tax, or financial advice. It does not know your local scheduling-notice, break or minor-labor laws. See how to make an employee schedule for the method, and do I need to hire another employee? for testing a hire before you post the job. Checking payroll against sales? See labor cost percentage by day. Worried about close-then-open shifts? See what a rest gap costs, or how to reduce overtime in a schedule.

Your people

Availability is days and hours separated by semicolons: Mon-Fri 9-17; Sat 10am-2pm; Sun off. Days you do not list count as unavailable; leave it blank or write any for always free. Max hours default to 40.

Shifts to cover

Days can be a range (Mon-Fri) or a list (Mon/Wed/Fri). Times can be 9, 9:30 or 9am. An end at or before the start runs overnight into the next day. People needed makes that many separate shifts. To lock a shift to someone, add fixed: Ana as a last cell (use fixed: Ana + Ben to pin two copies); the tool plans everyone else around it.

Sets each person's prev: (when their last shift ended) so rest rules hold across Monday.

Your people, shifts and settings are remembered on this device only (browser local storage), so next week you can open the page and click the button.

Enter your people and shifts, then click the button.

Collect your team's availability

Stop chasing availability in group chats. Make a link, send it to your team, and each person fills a week grid and sends you one line back. Paste the lines below and they replace each person's availability in your staff list; wages, roles and the hours cap you set stay (a person can only lower their own max hours). The link carries only the business name, week and, if you add it, one person's name; nothing is stored or uploaded.

Result

The roster

Hours and pay by person

PersonShiftsHoursOvertimePayrollAgainst their limits

Who this week depends on

Re-builds the week without each person. If shifts then go uncovered, that person is a single point of failure.

Changes since you posted it

Posted a schedule, then changed it? Choose the roster CSV you posted, say when you made the change, and see every shift that was added, cancelled or moved, how much notice each got, and the premium pay your own rule would owe. Fair-workweek laws differ by city and change: enter your window and premium from the rule that applies to you; nothing here is a statement of what a law requires.

Someone called in sick? Who can take the shift

Pick a shift. It lists everyone who could take it without touching anyone else's week, cheapest first, and why the rest cannot.

Someone out for several days? Re-cover all their shifts

Pick the person and the days they are out. Every shift they hold on those days goes to someone else, cheapest first, without moving anyone else's existing shifts. Shifts nobody can take stay open, with the reason.

Days out (none ticked = the whole week)

Against filling shifts in listed order

What you get by going through the shifts in time order and giving each to the first person in your list who is free and within the rules.

PlanShifts left openOvertime hoursPayroll
No pay or wages on it, so it is safe to post in the break room.

How it is calculated

Hard rules (never broken): a person is only given a shift that falls inside one of their availability windows for the whole shift; shifts for one person never overlap and leave at least your rest gap between them; weekly hours stay at or under their maximum; days in a row stay at or under your limit. Objective: first cover as many shift-hours as possible, then minimise real payroll (wage × (1 + extras), overtime hours above your threshold at the multiplier), plus a small penalty for each hour a person is under their minimum and a quadratic penalty for hours drifting from a fair share (the balance slider). Search: a greedy build that fills the most constrained shifts first, then seeded simulated annealing with reassign and swap moves over several restarts; a fixed seed makes it repeatable. On small problems the tests compare it with an exhaustive search of every roster and it finds the same optimum; on large ones it is a strong heuristic, not a proof.

Not modelled: predictive-scheduling and fair-workweek notice rules, meal and rest breaks, minor-labor limits, split-shift premiums, skills or roles, tips, union rules, seniority, time off requests across weeks (one week's time off works: add off: Wed; Fri 5pm-close to a person; a soft wish works too: prefer: Sat gives that person those hours when it costs nothing; avoid: Sat; Fri 5pm-close keeps those hours free unless the roster would otherwise leave a shift open or cost more). The rest rule does carry over from last week if you add prev: Sun 10pm to a person (when their last shift ended). Unverified: checked against exhaustive search and invented data in unit tests, not against a real operator's payroll or a scheduling law.

Common questions

How do I make an employee schedule that covers every shift?

List each shift you need covered with how many people it takes, list each person with their availability, weekly hour limits and wage, and assign people to shifts one hard rule at a time: available for the whole shift, not double-booked, enough rest since their last shift, under their weekly limit. This tool does that search for you and shows any shift it could not fill with the reason.

How does the roster builder decide who works which shift?

It never breaks a hard rule (availability, weekly hour cap, rest between shifts, consecutive days, no double-booking). Among the rosters that follow those rules it covers as many shifts as possible first, then picks the lowest payroll, counting overtime above your threshold, nudged by the hour balance slider and by each person's minimum hours. The search is a seeded simulated-annealing optimiser, so the same inputs always give the same roster.

Is the roster guaranteed to be the cheapest possible?

No. Choosing who works which shift is a hard combinatorial problem, so the tool searches rather than proves optimality. On small problems the test suite checks the result against an exhaustive search of every possible roster and it matches. On a full week it finds a strong roster quickly, and the result is deterministic so you can compare changes fairly.

What does the hour balance slider do?

At zero the tool chases the lowest payroll, which can pile hours on the cheapest people and leave others under their minimum. Raising it adds a penalty for each person's hours drifting from their fair share of the total, in proportion to their weekly limit. Payroll shown is always the real cost, not the penalised score.

What does who-is-critical mean?

For each person on the roster the tool re-builds the week without them and reports how many hours of shifts would then go uncovered. A person whose absence leaves hours uncovered is a single point of failure: one sick call and a shift is open. Use it to see where you need a backup or wider availability.

What rules and laws does it check?

It enforces the availability, weekly hour limit, rest gap and consecutive-day limit that you type in, and prices weekly overtime above the threshold you set, plus optional daily overtime and double time (California-style presets included). It does not know your local predictive-scheduling or fair-workweek notice rules, break and meal-period rules, minor-labor limits, union terms or tip rules, which vary by place. Check the roster against the rules that apply to you.

Is my staff list uploaded anywhere?

No. Names, wages and availability are read and solved in this browser tab. Nothing is sent to a server, there are no accounts or cookies, and the tool does not store your roster. It works offline once the page has loaded.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional or your own knowledge of the labor rules that apply to you. Results are planning estimates from the numbers you supply. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it.

Independent. Not affiliated with any scheduling, payroll or point-of-sale vendor, and none is named or ranked here.

labor-cost-percentage-by-day.html.text:
← Shift roster builder

Labor cost percentage: how to calculate it, by week and by day

Labor cost percentage is payroll divided by sales for the same period. The formula is easy. The useful part is doing it for each day of the schedule you are about to post, because the weekly number averages away the days that lose money.

Open the free roster builder

The formula

Labor % = scheduled payroll ÷ projected sales × 100. Scheduled payroll is hours times each person's wage, plus any overtime premium, plus payroll taxes and benefits if you want the full cost. Projected sales is your forecast for the same days, usually last year's or last month's matching week.

A worked example

An invented café has seven people. The roster builder schedules 216 hours for a payroll of $3,622, and three shifts stay open. Two possible weeks:

Projected weekly salesLabor %Against a 30% target
$14,00025.9%$578 under the $4,200 limit
$12,00030.2%$22 over the $3,600 limit

Now enter daily sales of $1,500, $1,600, $1,700, $1,900, $2,600, $3,200 and $2,400 (Monday to Sunday):

DayHoursPayrollSalesLabor %
Mon32$548$1,50036.5%
Tue35$604$1,60037.8%
Wed35$594$1,70034.9%
Thu35$604$1,90031.8%
Fri27$470$2,60018.1%
Sat28$434$3,20013.6%
Sun24$368$2,40015.3%

Tuesday is the worst day at 37.8%, and the weekend runs at about half that. The week as a whole looks acceptable, but staffing is thickest on the quietest days. Moving hours from the early week to Friday and Saturday, within each person's availability and limits, is a decision the daily view makes visible. Daily payroll excludes the overtime premium, which is priced weekly.

Try it with your own week

Questions

What is a good labor cost percentage?

There is no single right number. It depends on the kind of business, how much of your service is labor versus product, and your prices. Compare against your own past weeks first; published industry ranges differ by source and should be treated as a rough check, not a target.

Should labor cost include payroll taxes and benefits?

Usually yes if you want the true cost of a shift. Wages alone understate it. The roster builder lets you add a burden percentage on top of wages; use the rate your accountant gives you.

Why look at labor percentage by day instead of by week?

A week can sit under target while the quiet days run far over it and the busy days run far under. The daily view shows which shifts to trim and where an extra person pays for themselves.
